turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come on in, sit yourself down. The nurse has the dressing off. What's wrong with the wound?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's red and there's stuff leaking out of it. I'm really worried, is it serious?
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): When was the caesarean?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ten days ago. Elective section, and the parking was a nightmare that morning, but the operation itself was grand.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): Redness started when?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Yesterday morning. I had a look and the skin round the scar was red, and I nearly rang the surgery there and then.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Discharge?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, yellow, from the bottom of the scar. A small bit yesterday, and there's more on the pad today.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pain?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): It's very sore, a throbbing, and it's worse if I move. Are the stitches going to give way?
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Temperature?
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's been hot the last two nights. She was shivering, and I had to fetch a blanket.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I only felt hot last night, I was not shivering, I was just warm and a bit wrecked. We hadn't a thermometer.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): Vomiting?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Cough? Pain passing water?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No cough. Waterworks are grand.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Heavy bleeding from below?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Only the light flow you'd expect, and that's easing.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Antibiotic after the section?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, co-amoxiclav, six hundred and twenty-five milligrams, three times a day, by mouth.
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): How many days?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Five days... or was it seven? Um, I finished the packet anyway. I think.
[SEG0024] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The box said seven days. She finished them three days ago.
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): Did it? I was thinking five. I've left the box at home, so I can't check.
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): Other tablets?
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Paracetamol, two of the five-hundred milligram ones, every four hours, by mouth.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah now, that's not right. I only took two doses yesterday, a thousand milligrams each time, for the heat. I skipped the night.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): Drug allergies?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None that I know of.
[SEG0031] person_1 (DOCTOR): Temperature thirty-eight point two. Pulse ninety-eight. Blood pressure one-eighteen over seventy-four. Saturations ninety-eight percent. Respiratory rate sixteen.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wound shows redness about three centimetres either side, yellow discharge at the lower end, tender to touch. It is not opening. Abdomen is soft, no guarding.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): So is it infected? Am I going to be alright, and is the baby in danger?
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'd say it's a superficial wound infection.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that serious? Do I have to go back into hospital today? I don't want to leave him.
[SEG0036] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not today. Wound swab, and bloods, full blood count and CRP.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the swab hurt? When do the bloods come back? What if they're bad?
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Swab is a quick wipe. I'm starting flucloxacillin, five hundred milligrams, four times a day, for seven days, by mouth.
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): Is that alright with breastfeeding? Will it upset him? What if I miss a dose?
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's used in breastfeeding. Start it today, on an empty stomach, an hour before food.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): If the swab grows something else, will you change the tablet again? I hate chopping and changing.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): We might, once we have the result. Take ibuprofen as well, four hundred milligrams three times a day, by mouth, with food.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I've never taken that with an antibiotic. Is it too much on the stomach? Can I still use the paracetamol?
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes to both. Paracetamol a thousand milligrams, up to four times a day, at least four hours apart.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): Can I shower? The midwife said lukewarm water. Can I put cream on it?
[SEG0046] person_1 (DOCTOR): Shower, no bath. No creams. Pat it dry and a fresh dressing once a day.
[SEG0047] person_2 (PATIENT): What if it gets worse tonight? I'm anxious about being at home with this.
[SEG0048] person_1 (DOCTOR): If the redness spreads quickly, or you vomit, or you feel faint, go to the emergency department.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Would they keep me? Should someone come with me?
[SEG0050] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bring someone. They'd assess you there. Most of these settle on tablets.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): How long till the scar looks normal? I keep thinking it'll be ruined, which is vain, I know.
[SEG0052] person_1 (DOCTOR): Too early to say about the scar. Treat the infection. It often settles in a few days.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's barely slept, doctor. Will you give her something for the worry?
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want a tablet for that. I'm worried, that's all. I just need to know it won't go into the blood.
[SEG0055] person_1 (DOCTOR): No sign of that today. Watch the red flags I gave you.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Do I check the temperature overnight? What number is too high?
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Check it if you feel hot. Come back sooner if it's up over thirty-eight point five and you're worse.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): And do I come back here anyway? When, like?
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Yes. I want you back in two days, in this clinic, either way.
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Will the swab be back by then? What if it isn't?
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): We may have an early look at it. If not, we still check the wound. Reception will book the two days.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
